items.descriptionAdvanced: Mesa Verde National Park in southwestern Colorado preserves the exceptional archaeological heritage of the Ancestral Puebloan people, who inhabited the region for over 700 years beginning around 600 CE. The park is world-famous for its well-preserved cliff dwellings, such as Cliff Palace and Spruce Tree House, which are built directly into the sheltered canyon walls. These elaborate masonry structures represent one of the most sophisticated examples of pre-Columbian architecture in North America. By the late 13th century, for reasons still debated by archaeologists—likely involving drought and resource exhaustion—the Ancestral Puebloans migrated away from these mesa tops, leaving behind an invaluable blueprint of their highly organized society. History K6 — Ancestral Puebloan society and cliff dwelling architecture.

items.descriptionAdvanced: Cahokia Mounds, located near present-day Collinsville, Illinois, is the site of the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico. At its peak between 1050 and 1200 CE, Cahokia was a sprawling, highly organized metropolis that likely housed up to 20,000 residents, rivaling contemporary European cities in population. The site is best known for its massive man-made earthen mounds, including Monks Mound, the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. These structures supported religious, political, and social functions for the Mississippian culture. The sophistication of their urban planning and their extensive trade networks, which reached across the continent, demonstrate the high level of development attained by these early North American societies. History K7 — Mississippian urban planning and earthwork construction.

items.descriptionAdvanced: Jamestown, established in 1607, was the first permanent English settlement in North America. Located in Virginia, it was a perilous enterprise that suffered from disease, starvation, and conflict with the Indigenous Powhatan Confederacy during its early years. The arrival of John Rolfe and his introduction of tobacco as a cash crop finally brought economic stability, fundamentally changing the colonial landscape and labor market through the early introduction of indentured servitude and the subsequent enslavement of Africans. Jamestown served as the capital of the Virginia Colony for nearly a century and remains a foundational site for understanding the birth of English colonial governance and the complex, often traumatic, social dynamics of early America. History K8 — English colonization and the tobacco cash economy.
